items.title: Variables, zero values, and short declaration
items.overview: Go has no uninitialised memory: every declared value starts at its type’s zero value — 0, "", false, nil. `var` declares with an explicit type and works at package level; `:=` infers the type and only works inside a function.
items.practicePrompt: Without AI, declare one of each: an int, a string, a bool, a slice, a map and a pointer. Print every zero value, then show which two panic when you write to them before make or new.
checklist: Name the zero value of every built-in type
Explain why a nil map reads fine but panics on write
Say when := is illegal and var is required
items.youtubeSearch: Go variables zero values short declaration
items.whyGoogle: Zero-value reasoning is the fastest way to spot a nil-map or nil-pointer bug in a coding round before the code ever runs.

items.title: Control flow: if, for, and switch
items.overview: Go has one loop keyword. `for` covers the classic, while-style, infinite and range forms; `if` takes an optional init statement that scopes the variable to the branch; `switch` needs no break and can switch on no expression at all.
items.practicePrompt: Without AI, rewrite a three-branch if/else chain as an expressionless switch, then write the same loop three ways: classic, while-style and range.
checklist: Write for as a while and as an infinite loop
Use if err := f(); err != nil to scope err
Explain fallthrough and why it is rare
items.youtubeSearch: Go for loop if switch tutorial
items.whyGoogle: Interviewers read fluency from loop and error-scoping idioms long before the algorithm is finished.

items.title: Functions, multiple returns, and closures
items.overview: Functions are values. Multiple returns carry the (result, error) convention, named results document intent, and closures capture variables rather than copies — which is exactly what makes loop-variable capture a classic bug.
items.practicePrompt: Without AI, write a counter constructor that returns a closure, then a function returning (value, error) and handle it with the comma-err idiom. Show what a closure captures when created inside a loop.
checklist: Return (T, error) and handle it at the call site
Explain what a closure captures, and when that bites
Pass a function as an argument to another function
items.youtubeSearch: Go functions multiple return values closures
items.whyGoogle: Callback and comparator arguments show up in sort, retry and memoisation questions, and the (T, error) shape is expected in every Go answer.

items.title: Constants and iota
items.overview: Constants are compile-time values and untyped by default, so an untyped constant adapts to the context it is used in. `iota` numbers a const block, which is how Go writes enums — there is no enum keyword.
items.practicePrompt: Without AI, declare a Status enum with iota plus a String() method, then find one case where an untyped constant compiles but the same value held in a typed variable does not.
checklist: Explain untyped vs typed constants
Write an iota enum with a String method
Say why Go has no enum keyword
items.whyGoogle: State machines in coding and design rounds read far better with a real enum than with bare ints.

items.title: Package layout and exported names
items.overview: Capitalized identifiers are exported. Keep packages cohesive; internal/ hides implementation from other modules.
items.practicePrompt: Attempt without AI: sketch package layout for a tiny URL service (handlers, store, model) with one paragraph rationale.
checklist: Name packages by purpose not util
Minimize exported surface area
Use internal for private modules
items.whyGoogle: Readable structure mirrors how Google organizes large Go repos.

items.title: Numeric types, conversion, and overflow
items.overview: Go has no implicit numeric conversion: int, int64 and float64 are distinct types and every mix needs an explicit cast. int is 64-bit on the platforms you will use, integer division truncates, and signed overflow wraps silently.
items.practicePrompt: Without AI, write mid := lo + (hi-lo)/2 and explain the overflow it avoids, then convert an int to float64 and back and show exactly where precision is lost.
checklist: Convert between int, int64 and float64 explicitly
Explain integer division and truncation
Name the overflow-safe midpoint formula
items.youtubeSearch: Go numeric types conversion integer overflow
items.whyGoogle: Binary search and sum questions are graded partly on whether you reach for the overflow-safe form by reflex.

items.title: Strings, runes, and range loops
items.overview: Strings are immutable UTF-8 byte sequences. range over string yields runes with byte indices. Use utf8/unicode packages for validation.
items.practicePrompt: Without AI, implement reverse words in a string handling Unicode spaces; test with multi-byte characters.
checklist: Distinguish bytes vs runes
Use strings.Builder for concatenation in loops
Avoid indexing string by byte for user-visible chars
items.whyGoogle: Google products are global; UTF-8 mistakes fail interviews and production.

items.title: Arrays vs slices
items.overview: An array carries its length in its type and copies on assignment; a slice is a three-word header (pointer, len, cap) over an array, so copying it copies only the header. Almost all Go code uses slices, and knowing why is the point.
items.practicePrompt: Without AI, pass a [3]int and a []int to a function that mutates element 0, and explain the two different results. Then use copy() so the two no longer alias.
checklist: State how [3]int and []int differ as types
Show that array assignment copies the data
Use copy() to break aliasing
items.whyGoogle: Aliasing bugs from a shared backing array are the most common Go mistake in a timed round.

resources.label: Go blog: arrays, slices and strings

items.title: Slices: length, capacity, and sharing
items.overview: A slice is a view over an array. Length is visible elements; capacity is room from the underlying array header. Sub-slicing shares storage—mutations alias.
items.practicePrompt: Without AI, write a function that removes index i from a slice in O(1) amortized when order need not be preserved, and one that preserves order. Explain aliasing with a sub-slice example.
checklist: Explain len vs cap on append
Show when two slices share backing array
Avoid leaking large arrays via small subslices
items.whyGoogle: Google Go interviews often probe slice aliasing and append reallocation—common source of subtle bugs in services.

items.title: append and variadic patterns
items.overview: append may reallocate when len exceeds cap. Spread with append(s, other...). Preallocate with make([]T, 0, n) when size is known.
items.practicePrompt: Without AI, merge two sorted int slices into one sorted slice in O(n+m) using append efficiently.
checklist: Preallocate when n is known
Reassign slice header: s = append(s, x)
Explain growth factor behavior qualitatively
items.whyGoogle: Performance-sensitive Go code avoids unnecessary allocations in hot paths.

items.title: Maps: zero value, existence, and iteration order
items.overview: Maps are reference types with nil meaning 'no map'. The comma-ok idiom distinguishes missing keys from zero values. Iteration order is randomized.
items.practicePrompt: Attempt without AI first: implement word frequency from a string using map[string]int and handle punctuation your way.
checklist: Use v, ok := m[k] correctly
Never assume map iteration order in tests
Initialize with make before write
items.whyGoogle: Hash maps mirror DSA rounds; idiomatic Go map usage signals production readiness.

items.title: Pointers, structs, and method receivers
items.overview: Pointer receivers mutate and avoid copies for large structs. Value receivers are fine for small immutable types. Consistency on a type matters.
items.practicePrompt: Without AI, implement a linked-list Node with pointer-receiver Insert and explain when value receivers would copy too much.
checklist: Choose pointer vs value receiver deliberately
Avoid mixing receiver types without reason
Explain nil pointer receiver calls
items.whyGoogle: Receiver choices affect API stability and concurrency safety in reviews.

items.title: Embedding and composition
items.overview: Embedding promotes methods for delegation; prefer composition over inheritance analogies from OOP.
items.practicePrompt: Without AI, embed http.HandlerFunc or custom type to add logging to a handler type.
checklist: Understand promoted methods
Avoid embedding solely for syntax sugar
Document embedded type behavior
items.whyGoogle: Composition idioms replace classical inheritance discussion.

items.title: Interfaces and implicit satisfaction
items.overview: Types satisfy interfaces by implementing methods—no explicit implements keyword. Empty interface holds any value; prefer small interfaces at call sites.
items.practicePrompt: Without AI, define a Storage interface with Get/Put and two fake implementations; write a function that accepts Storage.
checklist: Keep interfaces small (io.Reader style)
Explain nil interface vs typed nil
Accept interfaces, return structs
items.whyGoogle: Interface design is central to testable Go at Google-scale codebases.

items.title: Type assertions and type switches
items.overview: x.(T) asserts interface dynamic type. Type switches dispatch on concrete types—useful for parsers and plugin shapes.
items.practicePrompt: Attempt without AI: parse []interface{} JSON-like values into Go types with a type switch and return descriptive errors.
checklist: Use comma-ok form to avoid panic
Prefer typed APIs over interface{} when possible
Document supported types in switches
items.whyGoogle: Shows you can work with semi-structured data without unsafe casts.

items.title: io.Reader and streaming
items.overview: Stream with io.Copy; limit reads with io.LimitReader. Compose with io.MultiReader and TeeReader.
items.practicePrompt: Without AI, implement handler that streams file to response with correct Content-Type and error handling.
checklist: Check Copy return values
Use LimitReader on uploads
Explain why loading whole file is risky
items.whyGoogle: Large-file handling distinguishes senior Go instincts.

items.title: Errors: values, wrapping, and errors.Is/As
items.overview: Errors are values. fmt.Errorf with %w wraps for inspection. errors.Is and errors.As replace fragile string comparisons.
items.practicePrompt: Attempt solo: create sentinel errors ErrNotFound and ErrInvalid; wrap in a repository layer and test with errors.Is.
checklist: Use %w for wrap chains
Prefer Is/As over == on wrapped errors
Document error semantics on exported APIs
items.whyGoogle: Clear error contracts matter in large monorepos and RPC boundaries.

items.title: defer, panic, and recover
items.overview: defer runs LIFO at function return. panic is for unrecoverable programmer errors; libraries should return errors. recover only inside deferred functions.
items.practicePrompt: Attempt without AI: write a defer that closes a file and logs close errors without overwriting the primary return error (outline approach in comments if stuck).
checklist: Use defer for close/unlock patterns
Do not use panic for normal control flow
Know recover scope limits
items.whyGoogle: Interviewers check whether you treat panic like exceptions in other languages.

items.title: Generics maps and slices helpers
items.overview: Go 1.18+ generics enable type-safe containers; prefer stdlib slices/maps packages when available.
items.practicePrompt: Attempt without AI: generic Map function transforming []T to []U; compare to pre-generics interface approach.
checklist: Use constraints.Ordered where needed
Avoid over-generic APIs
Know slices.Contains from stdlib
items.whyGoogle: Modern Go interviews may include generics in utility code.

items.title: Table-driven tests
items.overview: Slice of structs {name, input, want} loops t.Run for subtests. Keeps cases readable and parallelizable.
items.practicePrompt: Without AI, table-test a function that validates parentheses including edge cases empty string and nested.
checklist: Name subtests descriptively
Use t.Parallel where safe
Compare with cmp.Diff or reflect.DeepEqual knowingly
items.whyGoogle: Google Go style strongly favors table tests in review.

items.title: Testing with interfaces and fakes
items.overview: Depend on interfaces; inject fakes in tests. Avoid testing unexported details—test behavior through public API.
items.practicePrompt: Attempt without AI: Service with Clock interface; fake clock to test timeout logic without sleeping.
checklist: Inject dependencies via constructor
Keep fakes in _test package or same package
Assert on behavior not call counts unless needed
items.whyGoogle: Testability is a hiring signal for production Go.

items.title: Benchmarks and profiling basics
items.overview: testing.B loops b.N times. go test -bench and -cpuprofile find hot spots. Read alloc counts in results.
items.practicePrompt: Attempt without AI: benchmark two string concat approaches (+= vs Builder) and interpret ns/op and allocs.
checklist: Reset timer if setup is heavy
Compare benchmarks on same machine load
Know pprof entry points at high level
items.whyGoogle: Performance culture at Google ties to measurement, not guessing.

items.title: Goroutines and the GOMAXPROCS model
items.overview: Goroutines are lightweight; the scheduler multiplexes them onto OS threads. Starting goroutines without lifecycle control leaks work.
items.practicePrompt: Without AI, launch N workers that square numbers and send results on a channel; main collects all results.
checklist: Every goroutine should have an exit path
Explain M:N scheduling at high level
Avoid unbounded goroutine creation
items.whyGoogle: Concurrency questions separate candidates who only know syntax from those who know lifecycle.

items.title: Channels: unbuffered vs buffered
items.overview: Unbuffered channels synchronize sender and receiver. Buffered channels decouple up to capacity; full send blocks.
items.practicePrompt: Attempt without AI: implement a bounded queue using a buffered channel with Enqueue/Dequeue semantics and document blocking behavior.
checklist: Close channels from sender side only
Range over channel until close
Pick buffer size with backpressure in mind
items.whyGoogle: Channel sizing and close semantics are frequent follow-ups in Go loops.

items.title: select for multiplexing
items.overview: select waits on multiple channel operations. default makes non-blocking attempts. Combine with context for cancellation.
items.practicePrompt: Without AI, merge two input channels into one output until both inputs close; use select.
checklist: Handle closed channels in receive
Use select with ctx.Done()
Avoid busy loops with default misuse
items.whyGoogle: Multiplexing mirrors event-driven servers and worker shutdown.

items.title: sync.WaitGroup for fan-in
items.overview: WaitGroup waits for a collection of goroutines. Add before start, Done in deferred cleanup, Wait after launches.
items.practicePrompt: Attempt without AI: fetch URLs concurrently (fake sleep) with WaitGroup and collect errors in a slice safely.
checklist: Pass WaitGroup by pointer
Avoid Add after Wait
Combine with errgroup for error propagation
items.whyGoogle: Fan-out/fan-in patterns appear in crawl and batch processing questions.

items.title: sync.Mutex and RWMutex
items.overview: Mutexes protect shared memory. RWMutex allows concurrent readers. Keep critical sections small; prefer channels when ownership is clear.
items.practicePrompt: Without AI, implement a thread-safe counter and a cache map with RWMutex; run with -race.
checklist: Lock/defer Unlock consistently
Do not copy Mutex
Explain mutex vs channel trade-off
items.youtubeSearch: Go sync Mutex RWMutex race detector
items.whyGoogle: Shared-state bugs are costly; Google expects -race awareness.

items.title: Race detector and data races
items.overview: go test -race finds unsynchronized access. Tests must exercise concurrent code paths to be useful.
items.practicePrompt: Attempt without AI: write a failing test that -race catches, then fix with mutex or channel.
checklist: Run -race in CI for concurrent packages
Understand happens-before intuitively
Do not rely on race detector in production
items.whyGoogle: Demonstrates production hygiene expected at Google.

items.title: sync.Once and singleton init
items.overview: sync.Once guarantees a function runs exactly once—common for lazy initialization.
items.practicePrompt: Without AI, lazy-init a config struct with Once and explain why double-checked locking is unnecessary in Go.
checklist: Store error from initialization
Do not nest Once incorrectly
Prefer explicit init in main when simple
items.whyGoogle: Shows knowledge of stdlib concurrency primitives beyond channels.

items.title: Atomic operations and sync/atomic
items.overview: atomic types for simple counters and flags when mutex is heavy; still understand visibility limits vs mutexes.
items.practicePrompt: Without AI: implement rate counter with atomic int64; discuss when mutex is safer.
checklist: Use atomic.AddInt64 etc.
Avoid mixing atomic and non-atomic access
Prefer mutex for compound invariants
items.whyGoogle: Low-level concurrency appears in performance-critical services.

items.title: context.Context cancellation
items.overview: Context propagates deadlines, cancellation, and request-scoped values. Pass ctx as first param; never store in structs long-term.
items.practicePrompt: Attempt without AI: HTTP handler calls a function that respects context cancel after 100ms simulated work.
checklist: Use context.WithTimeout for outbound calls
Check ctx.Err() in loops
Cancel releases resources via defer cancel()
items.whyGoogle: Google invented context—expect deep questions in Go backend interviews.

items.title: Worker pool pattern
items.overview: Fixed workers read jobs from a channel; results and errors need separate handling. Context cancels idle and in-flight work.
items.practicePrompt: Without AI, build a pool of 4 workers processing jobs with graceful shutdown on SIGINT outline using context.
checklist: Bound concurrency explicitly
Close job channel to signal no more work
Propagate first error or collect all
items.whyGoogle: Classic onsite coding prompt for Go-specialized teams.

items.title: errgroup with context
items.overview: golang.org/x/sync/errgroup runs goroutines with shared cancel on first error—cleaner than manual WaitGroup+error channels.
items.practicePrompt: Attempt without AI: parallel RPC stubs that fail fast when one returns error using errgroup.
checklist: Use derived context from errgroup
Limit parallelism with semaphore if needed
Wait returns first error
items.whyGoogle: Idiomatic pattern in Google Go code for parallel steps.

items.title: net/http Server and HandlerFunc
items.overview: Handler serves HTTP; ServeMux routes by pattern. Go 1.22+ improved method and path patterns—know your version semantics.
items.practicePrompt: Without AI, serve /health and /api/v1/items with two handlers using ServeMux.
checklist: Set timeouts on Server struct
Handle MethodNotAllowed where relevant
Log request ID from header or generate
items.whyGoogle: Many Google teams ship Go microservices behind gRPC or HTTP.

items.title: Middleware chains
items.overview: Middleware wraps handlers for logging, auth, recovery. Pattern: func(next http.Handler) http.Handler.
items.practicePrompt: Attempt without AI: compose logging and panic-recovery middleware around a business handler.
checklist: Preserve http.Handler interface
Pass context with request values
Return proper status on panic recovery
items.whyGoogle: Clean middleware shows you understand request-scoped concerns.

items.title: JSON encoding and validation
items.overview: json.NewEncoder(w).Encode for responses; Decoder for bodies. Struct tags control names; omit empty carefully.
items.practicePrompt: Without AI, POST handler decodes JSON, validates required fields, returns 422 with error list.
checklist: Limit request body size with MaxBytesReader
Set Content-Type on responses
Do not leak internal errors to clients
items.whyGoogle: REST JSON APIs remain common in interview exercises.

items.title: httptest for handlers
items.overview: httptest.NewRecorder and NewServer simulate requests without binding ports. Test status, headers, and body.
items.practicePrompt: Without AI, test a JSON handler for 200 and 400 paths using httptest.
checklist: Set Request method and body correctly
Table-test status codes
Close response bodies in client tests
items.whyGoogle: Backend rounds often include writing or testing HTTP handlers.

items.title: Graceful shutdown
items.overview: ListenAndServe in goroutine; signal.Notify for SIGTERM; Server.Shutdown with context drains connections.
items.practicePrompt: Attempt without AI: sketch main that shuts down within 10s on interrupt.
checklist: Use Shutdown not Close for drain
Cancel background workers on signal
Document readiness vs liveness
items.whyGoogle: Production readiness question in SRE-leaning loops.

items.title: database/sql connection pool
items.overview: sql.DB is a pool. Set MaxOpenConns, MaxIdleConns, ConnMaxLifetime. Always use context-aware QueryContext.
items.practicePrompt: Without AI, write a function GetUser(ctx, id) with QueryRowContext and map sql.ErrNoRows to domain error.
checklist: Defer rows.Close
Use prepared statements for hot queries
Ping on startup in main
items.whyGoogle: Data layer questions appear in full-stack Go interviews.

items.title: SQL NULL and sql.Null types
items.overview: Nullable columns map to sql.NullString, NullTime, etc. Distinguish NULL from zero value in Go.
items.practicePrompt: Attempt without AI: scan optional profile fields into struct with Null types and JSON output omitempty.
checklist: Check Valid field after Scan
Use pointers for optional JSON fields alternatively
COALESCE in SQL vs app defaults
items.whyGoogle: Schema reality includes NULL—interviews test edge cases.

items.title: Transactions and isolation
items.overview: BeginTx with options, defer Rollback, Commit on success. Keep transactions short; handle serialization failures with retry policy at app layer.
items.practicePrompt: Attempt without AI: transfer balance between two accounts in one transaction with row-level preconditions.
checklist: Rollback on any error before Commit
Use context timeout on Tx
Explain phantom vs write skew qualitatively
items.whyGoogle: Correct money-style updates test ACID understanding in Go.

items.title: Migrations and schema discipline
items.overview: Version schema with migration tools; backward-compatible deploys require expand-contract patterns.
items.practicePrompt: Without AI, write two SQL migrations adding a nullable column then backfilling—describe deploy order.
checklist: Never edit applied migration files
Index creation concurrency awareness
Test migrations on copy of prod shape
items.whyGoogle: Google emphasizes safe rollout even in interview discussions.

items.title: Configuration and twelve-factor env
items.overview: Read config from env with os.Getenv; parse durations and ints explicitly; fail fast on missing required vars.
items.practicePrompt: Without AI, Config struct loaded from env with validation and helpful error messages.
checklist: Document env vars in README
Separate config load from main logic
Use flags for local dev overrides only
items.whyGoogle: Deployable services need clear config boundaries.

items.title: Structured logging with log/slog
items.overview: slog emits leveled structured logs with key-value pairs. JSON handler suits production aggregation.
items.practicePrompt: Attempt without AI: add slog middleware logging method, path, status, duration_ms.
checklist: Use consistent attribute keys
Log errors with slog.Any("err", err)
Avoid logging secrets or PII
items.whyGoogle: Observability is part of 'production Go' expectations.

items.title: Health checks and readiness
items.overview: Liveness: process up. Readiness: dependencies OK. Kubernetes uses both for routing and restarts.
items.practicePrompt: Without AI, implement /live and /ready where ready checks DB Ping.
checklist: Keep liveness cheap
Timeout dependency checks
Return 503 on not ready
items.whyGoogle: Connects Go services to how Google runs containers at scale.

items.title: Multi-stage Docker builds for Go
items.overview: Build static binary with CGO_ENABLED=0 in builder stage; copy into distroless or scratch runtime.
items.practicePrompt: Attempt without AI: write Dockerfile for a tiny HTTP server under 20MB image.
checklist: Use go mod download layer cache
Run as non-root in final stage
Set GOOS/GOARCH explicitly if cross-building
items.whyGoogle: Take-homes and infra questions expect container basics.

items.title: Reading an unfamiliar codebase fast
items.overview: Orientation order that works under time pressure: entry points (main, handlers, cmd), then the request/data path, then the types that carry state, then the tests. Read names and signatures before bodies; a package's exported surface tells you its job faster than its internals do.
items.practicePrompt: Pick any Go repo you have never opened (try a mid-sized CLI on GitHub). In 20 minutes, write: the entry point, the three most important types, the data flow for one operation, and two questions you would ask the author. No AI for the first 20 minutes.
checklist: Name the entry point and the main data path before reading any function body
Write the invariant each core type maintains
List the packages you did NOT need to read, and why
Finish with two concrete questions, not a vague summary
items.youtubeSearch: reading unfamiliar codebase strategy software engineer
items.whyGoogle: Google's 2026 code-comprehension round hands you a 200–500 line codebase you did not write. Orientation speed is the scored skill.

items.title: Debugging by hypothesis, not by guessing
items.overview: State the hypothesis before you change anything: what you believe is wrong, what you expect to observe if it is, and the cheapest observation that would disprove it. Bisect the data path rather than reading top to bottom. A failing test is a better instrument than a print statement.
items.practicePrompt: Take a passing Go program, introduce a subtle bug (off-by-one, wrong map key, missed error return), hand it to yourself a day later, and fix it while narrating each hypothesis aloud. Time yourself.
checklist: Say the hypothesis out loud before editing
Find the smallest input that reproduces
Write the regression test before the fix
State how you know the fix is complete, not just that the symptom stopped
items.whyGoogle: The comprehension round scores debugging reasoning explicitly. Narrated hypotheses are what the interviewer can grade.

items.title: Working with an AI assistant, and verifying it
items.overview: In an assisted round the assistant is a fast, unreliable colleague. Use it for breadth (where is X handled, what calls this) and never for the final claim. Every answer it gives is a hypothesis you then confirm against the code, a test, or the type system. Unverified acceptance is the scored failure.
items.practicePrompt: On an unfamiliar Go repo, ask an assistant three breadth questions, then verify each answer yourself and write down which one it got wrong or oversimplified. If none were wrong, your questions were too easy.
checklist: Ask for locations and call paths, not for conclusions
State your own expectation before reading the answer
Verify every claim against the code or a test
Say out loud when you are rejecting the assistant's suggestion, and why
items.youtubeSearch: Google AI assisted coding interview Gemini code comprehension 2026
items.whyGoogle: Google's pilot scores prompt quality, output validation, and debugging. Verification out loud is the difference between a hire and a no-hire in this round.

items.title: Improving code you did not write
items.overview: After the bug is fixed, the round asks what you would improve. Good answers name a real risk and its cost: an unbounded goroutine, a missing context deadline, an error swallowed with _, a map shared without a lock, a test that asserts nothing. Bad answers rename variables.
items.practicePrompt: Review a 300-line Go file you did not write. Produce three improvements ranked by risk, each with the failure it prevents and what it would cost to make the change.
checklist: Name the failure each change prevents
Rank by risk, not by tidiness
Flag concurrency and lifetime issues before style
Say which change you would NOT make and why
items.youtubeSearch: Go code review best practices concurrency context
items.whyGoogle: Judgement about someone else's code is the daily reality of a large monorepo, and the closing question of the comprehension round.
